title: That Red Light Is Sensing Your Car's Metal #shorts
summary: Many actuated traffic signals use an inductive loop: wire in a saw cut, driven at 10-200 kHz; a vehicle stopped over it lowers the loop's inductance. Bikes and small motorcycles may not register, so Minnesota and Missouri give riders an affirmative defense (FHWA, state statutes).
tags: how do traffic lights know you're there
sources: Inductive loop: a slot is cut in the pavement and one or more turns of wire placed in it; the detector drives energy through the loop at 10 kHz to 200 kHz; a vehicle over or stopped within the loop decreases its inductance; the 6 x 6 ft square loop is the most commonly used for actuated signal control (FHWA Traffic Detector Handbook, FHWA-IP-90-002): https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/publications/research/safety/Ip90002/ip90002.pdf

Minnesota: affirmative defense for a bicycle or motorcycle that stops and faces a red light for an unreasonable time when the signal apparently failed to detect it and no vehicle or person is approaching (Minn. Stat. 169.06 subd. 9): https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/?id=169.06
Missouri: same affirmative defense for motorcycles and bicycles (RSMo 304.285): http://revisor.mo.gov/main/OneSection.aspx?section=304.285&bid=16255&hl=

Loops can miss vehicles not stopped over them; smaller vehicles like motorcycles may go undetected (Jalopnik, 28 Feb 2026, context): https://jalopnik.com/2108989/how-traffic-light-sensors-detect-cars/

scenes.narration: That red light knows you're there. There's a loop of wire cut into the road, right under your car.
A box drives a current through it, flipping up to {200,000|two hundred thousand} times a second.
Your car's metal changes the loop's field, and the box tells the controller: someone's waiting.
A bike or a small motorcycle may not have enough metal. So Minnesota and Missouri give riders a legal defense when a red never changes.
